edition.deck: A US-Russia diesel deal tests support for Ukraine as energy costs rise; other leading stories include the proposed livestream of a US military execution and a fresh challenge to the International Criminal Court.
edition.editorialNote: Grouped duplicate coverage of shared events, while preserving useful differences in analysis and testimony. Danish-language reporting has been translated into English; claims and unresolved details remain attributed to their sources.

content.headline: Trump says Russia will supply diesel in deal Zelenskyy calls a gift to Putin
content.shortHeadline: Trump’s Russian diesel deal draws fury from Zelenskyy
content.standfirst: The US president says the fuel will ease prices as the Iran war disrupts supplies. Zelenskyy says the deal will help fund Russia’s war, while the size and practical impact of the promised deliveries remain uncertain.

image.caption: US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin in 2025.

sources.originalTitle: Trump announces deal for Russian diesel as Zelensky calls it a gift to Putin
Zelenskyy furious as Trump announces deal to buy Russian diesel
Trump agrees deal with Putin to release Russian diesel to US and global markets
Trump køber diesel af Putin, og det huer ikke Zelenskyj: Giver Rusland penge at føre krig for
Analysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices
Ukraine war briefing: Kyiv blasts peace talks as just ‘smokescreen’ for Trump‘s Russian diesel deal

segments.body: Donald Trump says Russia will immediately supply 300,000 tonnes of diesel to US and global markets, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and a further one million tonnes. The US Treasury has issued a temporary licence allowing Russian diesel sales; Trump also described a possible additional three million tonnes, dependent on refinery conditions.

segments.title: A disputed route to lower fuel costs
segments.body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the deal an “investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged”. The announcement came as US, Ukrainian and European officials held talks in Miami. Trump says lower prices are a priority, but analysts cited by the BBC question whether Russia can deliver the quantities promised or whether they would make a material difference to US prices.

perspectives.body: The BBC’s North America correspondent frames the agreement as Trump’s most dramatic effort yet to ease fuel-price pressure before the midterms, while noting that voters may see little immediate relief.

content.headline: US plan to livestream Fort Hood execution draws condemnation
content.shortHeadline: US plan to livestream execution faces broad condemnation
content.standfirst: Nidal Hasan is scheduled to be executed by firing squad on 3 December, but officials have not settled how a livestream would work. Politicians, religious leaders and human-rights voices have challenged the plan.

image.caption: US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, who announced the livestream plan.

sources.originalTitle: JD Vance casts doubt on firing squad execution and says he will not watch it
Who is Nidal Hasan? What to know about US plans to livestream an execution online
‘Medieval’ and ‘disturbing’: US plan to livestream execution elicits global condemnation
Pete Hegseth’s plan to livestream execution puts US in dubious company
Pentagon: Henrettelse af mand bag massedrab på militærbase skal livestreames
Execution live stream could cause PTSD in viewers, say psychiatrists
Hegseth’s firing squad shows the cruelty at the heart of Trump’s White House

segments.body: The Pentagon says the execution of Nidal Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009, is planned for 3 December and will be livestreamed. President Donald Trump has said he approves of the plan, while Vice-President JD Vance has questioned whether it will happen. The details of any broadcast remain unclear.

segments.title: Questions about spectacle and harm
segments.body: The UN human rights office has warned that broadcasting an execution would breach the prohibition of torture; critics in both US parties have also objected. Reporting in the Guardian and i Paper records competing arguments: experts warn of distress and possible propaganda value, while one death-penalty specialist says a broadcast could increase transparency around the process.

perspectives.body: Psychiatrists cited by the Guardian warn that viewers could experience distress, particularly people with existing mental-health difficulties; one recommends that mainstream media not transmit the images or sounds.

content.headline: US sanctions on ICC condemned as an assault on the rule of law
content.shortHeadline: US sanctions target the International Criminal Court
content.standfirst: Washington’s measures target the court as an institution, not just individual officials. The ICC says it will not be deterred, while member states including the UK have reaffirmed their support.

sources.originalTitle: US unveils sanctions on ICC in move court condemns as 'assault on rule of law'

segments.body: The Trump administration has announced sanctions aimed at preventing US entities from providing goods or services to the International Criminal Court, including banking and software. The ICC calls the measures an assault on the rule of law. Some provisions have a six-month grace period, during which member states can continue paying for the court’s operations.

segments.title: Possible consequences for cases
segments.body: The UK joined Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan and the Netherlands in saying they strongly disagree with the sanctions and continue to support the court. A legal expert cited by the BBC warns that if the ICC cannot conduct fair trials or appeals, detainees awaiting trial or judgment could ultimately have to be released. The full effect of the sanctions is not yet clear.

content.headline: Hurricane Isaias makes landfall in Florida as dangerous flooding looms
content.shortHeadline: Hurricane Isaias hits Florida; evacuations and outages reported
content.standfirst: The category 2 storm brought powerful winds ashore in the Florida Panhandle, with officials warning of dangerous surge, flooding and possible tornadoes. Hundreds of thousands of customers were reported without power.

image.caption: An empty beach on Mon Louis Island, Alabama, on 9 October 2026.

sources.originalTitle: Life-threatening Hurricane Isaias makes landfall in Florida
Hurricane Isaias makes landfall in Florida with severe effects expected across several states

segments.body: Hurricane Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, on Friday evening, with winds reported at about 105 mph. Forecasters warned of severe effects along the northern Gulf coast and inland, including life-threatening storm surge. Florida, Alabama and Mississippi declared states of emergency, and some coastal residents were told to evacuate.

segments.title: Disruption spreads inland
segments.body: Nearly 500,000 customers in Alabama and Florida had lost power by Friday evening, according to the Guardian report. Flights were grounded at several Panhandle airports, and emergency teams were positioned to assist. The storm was expected to weaken after landfall, but warnings covered areas well beyond the coast.

content.headline: Ebola patient crossed three countries before infection was identified
content.shortHeadline: Ebola case exposes gaps in regional screening
content.standfirst: A Kenyan businessman travelled through DR Congo and Uganda while ill before his infection was confirmed in Nairobi, where he later died. Health authorities are tracing contacts across borders.

image.caption: Potential contacts of the Ebola patient have been placed under quarantine in Nairobi.

sources.originalTitle: Questions remain over Ebola patient who travelled across three nations undetected

segments.body: Africa CDC reconstructed nearly six weeks of travel by a 40-year-old Kenyan man who had lived and travelled in DR Congo before crossing into Uganda and flying to Nairobi. His Ebola infection was identified only after he reached a Nairobi hospital; he died on 5 October. When and where he contracted the virus remains unknown.

segments.title: Contact tracing continues
segments.body: The Kenyan government identified 66 people who may have had contact with the patient in Kenya, and the World Health Organization said the number could rise as tracing continues in Uganda and DR Congo. Health experts cited by the BBC say the case also highlights the limits of airport temperature checks: a person can be infected without registering a fever at screening.

content.headline: French school protests expose anger over overcrowding and staff shortages
content.shortHeadline: School protests reflect France’s wider political divide
content.standfirst: Students have taken to the streets over crowded classes, poor facilities and staff shortages. The unrest has become a political flashpoint, while arrests, injuries and disputed accounts of clashes deepen tensions.

image.caption: Students have protested across France over conditions in secondary schools.

sources.originalTitle: 'Everyone hates the police' – what France's school protests reveal about a divided nation

segments.body: Hundreds of thousands of students have protested across France since the end of last month, demanding better-resourced secondary schools. Pupils and teachers describe overcrowded classes, long days, broken facilities and too few staff. The government has promised 3,000 additional supply teachers and a plan by the end of October, but students say the response falls short.

segments.title: A dispute over policing and politics
segments.body: The interior ministry says nearly 7,000 people have been detained during the disorder, most of them children, and more than 700 police officers have been injured. Unions and rights groups also report injuries among pupils and accuse police of heavy-handed tactics. Accounts differ over how a 15-year-old boy lost his hand during a confrontation; police have since been barred from using stun grenades at school protests.

content.headline: Three killed in Houthi attacks on Riyadh airport, Saudi authorities say
content.shortHeadline: Houthi attacks kill three at Riyadh airport
content.standfirst: Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority says attacks struck the airport and a Saudia aircraft. The deaths come amid renewed fighting between the Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi-backed forces in Yemen.

sources.originalTitle: Three Saudi nationals killed in Houthi attacks on Riyadh airport

segments.body: Three Saudi nationals were killed in two attacks on Riyadh’s international airport, Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority said. One attack targeted the airport and another struck an aircraft belonging to state carrier Saudia; the airline said one of its pilots was among the dead. Air traffic later returned to normal.

segments.title: Wider fighting escalates
segments.body: Yemen’s Houthi group said it had launched two ballistic missiles at the airport. The latest deaths follow earlier fatal attacks on Saudi airports this week, as fighting intensifies between the Houthis and Yemen’s Saudi-backed government forces. The Houthis say their attacks respond to Saudi action in Yemen; Saudi Arabia has not confirmed all the targets claimed by the group.

content.headline: UAE prosecutor says co-pilot planned attack on Tel Aviv airport
content.shortHeadline: UAE prosecutor alleges co-pilot planned suicide attack
content.standfirst: The UAE says a Flydubai co-pilot intended to hijack a plane and crash it into a terminal after attacking the captain. The airline has not commented, and the account comes from a preliminary investigation.

image.caption: The Flydubai aircraft involved in the incident, pictured after its later arrival at Ben Gurion Airport.

sources.originalTitle: Emiraterne: Pilot ville udføre selvmordsangreb mod Tel Avivs lufthavn

segments.body: The United Arab Emirates’ top prosecutor says a preliminary investigation found that a Flydubai co-pilot intended to hijack a flight from Dubai to Israel and crash it into a terminal at Ben Gurion Airport. The prosecutor alleges the Omani pilot had studied the route on earlier flights and was inspired by the 11 September 2001 attacks in the United States.

segments.title: Incident under investigation
segments.body: The incident occurred on 30 September, according to the prosecutor. The co-pilot allegedly attacked the captain with an axe; passengers intervened, and two pilots travelling as passengers landed the aircraft in Saudi Arabia. Flydubai has not commented on the prosecutor’s account.

content.headline: Labour holds Starmer’s former seat as Greens face questions over defeat
content.shortHeadline: Labour wins Holborn as Green leader faces internal pressure
content.standfirst: Sagal Abdi-Wali won 45% of the vote, beating Green leader Zack Polanski in a low-turnout contest. The result keeps Labour’s seat but leaves the Greens debating their direction after a divisive conference motion.

image.caption: Sagal Abdi-Wali celebrates after winning the Holborn and St Pancras by-election.

sources.originalTitle: Labour hails byelection win as return of leftwing voters after Starmer era
‘The real deal’: Sagal Abdi-Wali’s journey from child refugee to Labour MP in former PM’s seat
Polanski’s leadership is in crisis. The divided Greens face an uncertain future
Does Polanski have to go? Greens at the crossroads after Holborn and St Pancras
‘Polanksi should go’: How hard-left revolt and antisemitism row turned Greens ‘toxic’
Polanski must resign after by-election loss, says leader of Jewish Greens

segments.body: Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali won the Holborn and St Pancras by-election with 45% of the vote, ahead of Zack Polanski on 33%. Turnout was 38.7%. Abdi-Wali, who came to the UK from Somalia as a child, said she wanted her election to show that people from backgrounds like hers belong in Britain.

segments.title: Pressure on Polanski
segments.body: The loss has intensified criticism of Polanski for missing a Green Party conference vote on a motion equating Zionism with racism while campaigning in the constituency. Vivien Lichtenstein, chair of Jewish Greens, called for him to resign; other senior Greens have criticised the motion or urged reform, while Polanski says members will decide his future.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s analysis says the defeat does not erase the Greens’ recent electoral growth, but argues Polanski now faces the twin challenge of rebuilding wider appeal and resolving internal divisions.

content.headline: Northern Ireland secretary bans contested Drumcree parade
content.shortHeadline: Drumcree parade banned after 13-day standoff
content.standfirst: Chris Bryant said the march through Portadown was not in the public interest after police warned of a risk of serious injury and disorder. The decision brought relief to residents but drew sharp criticism from unionist leaders.

image.caption: A police vehicle near Drumcree church in Portadown.

sources.originalTitle: Northern Ireland secretary Chris Bryant bans Drumcree parade

segments.body: Northern Ireland Secretary Chris Bryant has banned the Orange Order parade along Portadown’s contested Garvaghy Road. The decision followed a 13-day standoff and advice from the police chief that proceeding carried an unacceptable risk of serious injury, disorder and wider tensions.

segments.title: Relief and dispute over the decision
segments.body: Residents welcomed the ban, which they said brought relief after a tense impasse. DUP leader Gavin Robinson said the decision bowed to republican pressure and undermined the rule of law. The Irish government welcomed it while urging both sides to avoid triumphalism and seek common ground.

content.headline: King pays £1.5m Royal Lodge repair bill for Andrew
content.shortHeadline: King pays Andrew’s £1.5m Royal Lodge bill
content.standfirst: The Crown Estate says it has received the net cost of repairs after Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor surrendered his lease. The payment comes as a court has ruled that warrants used in the police investigation were unlawful.

image.caption: Royal Lodge, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor’s former home in Windsor.

sources.originalTitle: King pays Andrew's £1.5m repair bill on Royal Lodge
Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor faced £1.8m repair bill after leaving Royal Lodge
Andrew should still be worried, even if the police investigation falters

segments.body: King Charles has paid the £1.5m net bill for repairs to Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor’s former home at Royal Lodge, according to the BBC. The Crown Estate says it received the money and did not pay Andrew compensation; the £1.8m repair bill was offset by about £300,000 due for the early surrender of his lease.

segments.title: Legal questions remain
segments.body: The payment follows Andrew’s successful challenge to the search warrants used by Thames Valley police, which a High Court judge ruled were obtained under the wrong legal provision. The police investigation into alleged misconduct in public office continues. Andrew has denied wrongdoing connected to Jeffrey Epstein.

content.headline: UK review warns of future risk of ADHD and autism overdiagnosis
content.shortHeadline: Review flags future risk as ADHD diagnoses rise
content.standfirst: A government-commissioned review says diagnoses among some young people are nearing or exceeding estimated prevalence, but says current evidence does not prove overdiagnosis is already widespread. It recommends changing how support is accessed.

image.caption: Professor Peter Fonagy’s review examines rising diagnoses and young people’s mental health.

sources.originalTitle: The four reasons why ADHD experts fear the UK is heading towards overdiagnosis
ADHD wait lists, benefits and medication need overhauling, landmark review says
How claims of ‘masking’ in ADHD are impacting diagnosis

segments.body: The review led by Professor Peter Fonagy says ADHD and autism diagnoses have risen sharply and warns that the current system, which often makes diagnosis the route to support, is not sustainable. It does not conclude that overdiagnosis is happening at scale, but identifies a serious future risk if present trends continue.

segments.title: Support beyond diagnosis
segments.body: The review recommends faster support while people wait for assessment, stronger oversight of private clinics and a greater focus on needs rather than diagnosis alone. It also discusses the possible effects of social media and smartphone use on distress and attention, while noting that digital technology can benefit some neurodivergent children. The proposed changes and their practical effects remain uncertain.

perspectives.body: The i Paper’s reporting stresses that experts disagree about where the balance lies: rising rates prompt concern about overdiagnosis, but the review does not establish that it is already occurring at scale.

content.headline: BBC faces talent losses as it plans more than 2,000 job cuts
content.shortHeadline: BBC cuts raise fears of losing experienced staff
content.standfirst: The corporation plans to cut more than 2,000 jobs as it seeks £500m in savings. Staff quoted by the i Paper warn that voluntary redundancies could drive away experienced people, while management says difficult choices are needed.

image.caption: The BBC is planning more than 2,000 job cuts across television and radio.

sources.originalTitle: BBC faces losing its best talent from news and sport as a result of savage cuts

segments.body: The BBC plans more than 2,000 job cuts across television and radio as it tries to close a funding gap and save £500m. Staff quoted by the i Paper say morale is low and warn that voluntary redundancy may prompt skilled employees to leave for other organisations.

segments.title: Programming changes
segments.body: The broadcaster has announced cuts to several Radio 4 programmes, with reduced commissioning on Radio 5 Live; the i Paper also reports that BBC Three and BBC Scotland broadcast channels could close. BBC Sounds director Jonathan Wall says the decisions are difficult and combine savings with investment for the future.

content.headline: Right to Buy backlog threatens council housebuilding plans
content.shortHeadline: Right to Buy sales threaten council housing targets
content.standfirst: Councils expect a prolonged wave of home sales as they work through applications made after discounts were cut in 2024. The i Paper’s analysis says projected sales exceed the government’s expected replacements over the next two years.

image.caption: The analysis compares projected Right to Buy sales with the number of replacement homes expected.

sources.originalTitle: Council housebuilding plan thrown into disarray by Right to Buy surge

segments.body: Right to Buy sales jumped 90% last year to 14,275 after discounts were reduced, and councils are still processing a large backlog of applications. The i Paper’s analysis of council papers and responses indicates more than 14,000 homes could be sold this year and next, compared with 10,450 replacements expected by the government.

segments.title: Councils question how quickly homes can be replaced
segments.body: Birmingham reported about 5,000 applications awaiting processing, while other councils say sales are spread across several financial years. The government says reforms and investment will help councils build more social homes than are sold over the next decade. Housing experts quoted in the report warn that sales receipts alone may not cover replacement costs.

content.headline: Pharmacy closures leave some English patients long journeys for care
content.shortHeadline: Pharmacy closures deepen access gaps in England
content.standfirst: Fifty-one high-street pharmacies closed in England between January and August, including branches in areas designated as having a shortage of healthcare access. The closures can leave patients travelling far for medicines and advice.

image.caption: The report says pharmacy closures are making local access to medicines harder for some patients.

sources.originalTitle: The worst places to live if you are ill – where trips to chemists take an hour

segments.body: Analysis cited by the i Paper found that 51 pharmacies in England closed between January and August, including 31 supported by a scheme intended to protect access in shortage areas. It says nearly 10 million people have seen their local pharmacy close since 2016.

segments.title: Funding pressure
segments.body: In Long Rock, Cornwall, the nearest alternative after a closure can mean a 17-mile round trip and up to 80 minutes on public transport, the report says. Pharmacy representatives say real-terms funding has fallen since 2016 and argue that the government’s announced funding increase has not closed the sector’s estimated shortfall.

content.headline: UK-EU reset faces fresh hurdles over student fees and trade rules
content.shortHeadline: Brexit reset deal faces hurdles over fees and trade
content.standfirst: The UK hopes to link negotiations on European student tuition fees with access to the EU’s proposed “Made in Europe” rules. Disagreement among member states and a short negotiating window put that strategy in doubt.

image.caption: An electric-car charging station in Bochum, Germany, illustrating the EU trade debate over vehicle rules.

sources.originalTitle: The new EV threat to UK Brexit deal

segments.body: The UK’s hopes of negotiating access to the EU’s proposed “Made in Europe” scheme alongside lower tuition fees for European students have encountered resistance. The i Paper reports that several member states opposed delaying talks on fees, while divisions within the EU have made a trade deal this year uncertain.

segments.title: A narrow window for agreement
segments.body: EU sources cited by the paper say only two to four weeks remain to conclude possible agreements on food and drink, youth mobility and linking carbon markets ahead of a planned 20 November summit. The UK government says closer cooperation could bring economic gains, but the outcome of the talks is unresolved.

content.headline: Police review ordered after criticism of Kirkerup investigation
content.shortHeadline: Review ordered into handling of Kirkerup case
content.standfirst: A review found that police could not fully account for some criticised aspects of the investigation into the 2023 abduction of a 13-year-old girl. Experienced investigators from other forces and a national unit will now examine the work.

image.caption: A review will examine police work in the Kirkerup case.

sources.originalTitle: Politiets efterforskning i Kirkerup-sag skal undersøges

segments.body: Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen says a review of the Kirkerup investigation found that police could not fully explain some of the criticisms raised and that parts of the work could have been handled differently, faster or better. He will ask the National Police to arrange a peer review by experienced investigators from other districts and the National Special Crime Unit.

segments.title: Questions about the timeline
segments.body: The report says the suspect was identified as a possible perpetrator at about 9.30am, based partly on video showing his car near the scene, but was not arrested until 2.48pm. The victim was found alive. The convicted man was sentenced to life imprisonment in 2024 for offences including the abduction and assault, the murder of Emilie Meng and an assault on another teenager.

content.headline: Government pension plan would boost early retirement and cut senior pension
content.shortHeadline: Pension proposal shifts funding from senior pension
content.standfirst: The government’s draft budget would add funding to the Arne early-retirement pension while reducing spending on senior pension. Unions, patient groups and several parties object to changing support for people who are ill or worn down.

image.caption: Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen with Arne Juhl, whose name is associated with the Arne pension.

sources.originalTitle: Mette Frederiksens politiske kronjuvel får milliardindsprøjtning - nedslidte seniorpensionister betaler prisen

segments.body: The government’s proposal would increase funding for the Arne pension by 1.56 billion kroner in 2030 and reduce senior-pension spending by 800 million kroner. Senior pension is intended for people whose ability to work is substantially reduced; the government says it is reasonable to target that scheme more closely while improving access to early retirement.

segments.title: Opposition and coalition hurdles
segments.body: The Danish Nurses’ Council, the Arthritis Association and opposition parties have criticised the proposed change, arguing that people with long working lives and health problems could be unfairly reassessed for other jobs. The proposal requires agreement from parties in the senior-pension settlement, and Venstre says it will not support the model as presented.

content.headline: Russian TV airs disputed footage of September incident with Danish helicopter
content.shortHeadline: Denmark disputes Russian account of helicopter incident
content.standfirst: Russian state television has aired footage it says shows a Danish military helicopter near a Russian frigate. Denmark disputes the account, and DR says it is still checking the video’s authenticity and what it shows.

sources.originalTitle: Russisk tv-kanal har vist video, der angiveligt stammer fra signalblus-hændelse

segments.body: Russian state television has broadcast footage it says is from a 14 September encounter between the frigate Soobrazitelny and a Danish Fennec helicopter near Gedser. The clip does not show the firing of two flares reported during the incident. DR says the images alone do not establish how close the helicopter was or whether the footage is authentic.

segments.title: Competing accounts
segments.body: Danish authorities have said the helicopter stayed about 150 metres from the ship; Russia has claimed it flew closer than 50 metres and called its actions provocative. Denmark’s defence minister describes the broadcast as a Russian disinformation campaign, while DR’s defence correspondent says it may be an effort to cast doubt on Danish authorities and shape the public account of the incident.

content.headline: Danish fishing report finds thousands of tonnes of fish discarded
content.shortHeadline: Report finds widespread fish discards in Danish waters
content.standfirst: A DTU report estimates that nearly 6,700 tonnes of fish and shellfish were thrown back into the sea in parts of the Danish fleet last year, including about 2,000 tonnes illegally. The environment minister wants cameras on fishing vessels.

sources.originalTitle: Flere tusinde ton fisk bliver smidt ulovligt tilbage i havet, og ’langt de fleste dør’: 'Et kolossalt spild af liv'

segments.body: A new report from the Technical University of Denmark estimates that almost 6,700 tonnes of catch were discarded by parts of the Danish fishing fleet last year—about 17% of the catch studied. Nearly 2,000 tonnes were discarded illegally, the report says; many fish die after being caught in bottom trawls and returned to the sea.

segments.title: Monitoring and fishing methods
segments.body: The largest share of discards was reported in Kattegat fishing for Norway lobster, where small-mesh nets also catch other species. Environment Minister Maria Reumert Gjerding wants camera monitoring on vessels. The fishing association says it recognises the problem and supports cameras, but wants more flexibility to use gear that can sort unwanted catch more effectively.

content.headline: Denmark considers South Korean partnership to rebuild warship capacity
content.shortHeadline: South Korean shipyards proposed for Danish frigates
content.standfirst: A DR analysis argues that cooperation with South Korea could help Denmark procure new frigates and rebuild shipbuilding expertise. The country has lost its ability to build large ships since the closure of Lindø shipyard.

sources.originalTitle: ANALYSE Hvis Danmark skal bygge krigsskibe igen, bør vi måske hive sydkoreanerne til landet

segments.body: Denmark has a political ambition to regain the ability to build warships, but it no longer has the industrial capacity to construct large vessels. DR’s analysis points to South Korea’s Hyundai shipyard as a possible partner, citing its ability to shift people and expertise between civilian and military shipbuilding.

segments.title: Avoiding a one-off fleet
segments.body: The analysis says joint procurement could also reduce the risk of Denmark operating a unique frigate design that is costly to maintain and upgrade. A partnership might allow Danish ships to use equipment also adopted by allied fleets. No final supplier or construction arrangement is identified in the reporting.

content.headline: Proposed cut to home-based student grants worries Danish students
content.shortHeadline: Students fear losing home-based grant support
content.standfirst: A proposed reduction to grants for students living with parents could leave some young people without their monthly support. Students’ representatives say the benefit also helps cover books, transport and household costs.

image.caption: Student Catharina Zvenova Nissen is concerned about losing her grant.

sources.originalTitle: SU skrumper: Catharina vil ikke at være en byrde for sine forældre

segments.body: Catharina Zvenova Nissen, a 20-year-old occupational therapy student in Aarhus, fears losing or receiving a reduced home-based student grant under the government’s proposed savings. Her parents have limited incomes, and she says the grant helps her cover expenses without asking them to cut back elsewhere.

segments.title: More students live at home
segments.body: Data obtained by DR shows that one in four students still live with their parents at age 22, and one in ten at 24. The chair of the Danish Students’ Council says that challenges the idea that home-based grants are merely spending money for school pupils; students may also pay rent or contribute to food and study costs.

content.headline: Young disabled people describe stigma around sexuality and relationships
content.shortHeadline: Disabled young people challenge assumptions about sex
content.standfirst: A woman with cerebral palsy says a doctor directed questions about her sex life to her assistant rather than to her. A disability organisation says assumptions that disabled people are asexual can affect confidence and access to care.

image.caption: Astrid Siemens Lorenzen, a student who lives with cerebral palsy.

sources.originalTitle: Astrid har cerebral parese og vil gøre op med fordomme om sex: 'Det er egentlig ret voldsomt'

segments.body: Astrid Siemens Lorenzen, who has cerebral palsy and communicates using an eye-controlled computer, says a gynaecologist asked her assistant whether she was sexually active rather than addressing her directly. She says repeated assumptions about her sexuality left her feeling for years that she was not entitled to a sex life.

segments.title: Calls for more inclusive care
segments.body: William Korte, chair of the Association of Young People with Disabilities, says young disabled people can face outdated assumptions that they are asexual. The organisation has no figures on how common these experiences are, but Korte says they can leave people questioning whether it is acceptable to have sexual interests and relationships.

content.headline: England beat Greece 3-1 to take first-leg lead in World Cup play-off
content.shortHeadline: England take 3-1 lead over Greece in World Cup play-off
content.standfirst: Georgia Stanway opened the scoring and Maya Le Tissier netted her first England goal, but defensive lapses let Greece back into the tie. The Lionesses need to finish the job in Tuesday’s return leg.

image.caption: Sarina Wiegman has led England to back-to-back European titles.

sources.originalTitle: Greek takeaways: What did we learn from Lionesses' win?

segments.body: England won 3-1 away to Greece in the first leg of their Women’s World Cup qualifying play-off. Georgia Stanway scored the opener and Maya Le Tissier added her first international goal in the second half; England also gave debuts to Erica Meg Parkinson and Grace Fisk.

segments.title: A lead, but work to do
segments.body: Sarina Wiegman welcomed the win but said England were frustrated not to keep a clean sheet. Greece hit the crossbar before Kallisti Brouksair scored, after England errors, leaving the hosts with a route back into the tie. Wiegman said England need to be sharper with their final ball and show more than just a win.

content.headline: Everton are up for sale again as Friedkin Group tests the market
content.shortHeadline: Everton owners put club up for sale
content.standfirst: The Friedkin Group is seeking a way out less than two years after buying Everton. The sale comes after a fraught summer and leaves David Moyes hoping new owners will take the club forward.

image.caption: Everton chairman Dan Friedkin has not attended a match since the takeover in December 2024.

sources.originalTitle: Everton up for sale again - so what next as owners TFG look for a way out?

segments.body: The Friedkin Group has said it is effectively putting Everton up for sale. The group paid more than £400m for a 99.5% share in December 2024. Football finance expert Kieran Maguire told BBC Sport he expects it to seek £750m to £800m, with current debts of about £468m.

segments.title: A strained relationship
segments.body: Everton’s relationship with the owners deteriorated after a summer in which a proposed sale of teenager Harrison Armstrong to Nottingham Forest provoked fan anger, while departures and a failed move for Folarin Balogun left Moyes short of options. The manager said he learned of the potential sale when the news became public and was disappointed supporters faced another period of uncertainty.

segments.title: What comes next
segments.body: Maguire said Everton’s stadium, history and fanbase could appeal to prospective buyers, while a deal would still require approval under the Premier League’s owners’ and directors’ process. Moyes said he would welcome the right people taking the club forward and would tell any interested buyer that Everton is worth buying.

content.headline: Maresca backs Manchester City as club appeals financial-rule ruling
content.shortHeadline: Maresca backs Man City as club appeals ruling
content.standfirst: An independent commission found Manchester City guilty of breaches of Premier League financial regulations; the club has appealed. Enzo Maresca says he trusts City’s leadership, while Michael Carrick says the case affected him personally.

image.caption: Enzo Maresca has won each of his first five Premier League games in charge of Manchester City.

sources.originalTitle: Man City titles 'absolutely not' tainted - Maresca
I've got my own questions on Man City case - Carrick
Man City whistleblower to remain in witness protection

segments.body: Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca said he “completely trusts” the club’s owners and leadership and believes City will win their appeal. An independent commission found the club guilty of charges relating to breaches of Premier League financial regulations between 2009-10 and 2017-18. City has appealed, so the case is not resolved.

segments.title: Rivals want clarity
segments.body: Manchester United manager Michael Carrick said the case had affected him personally after City’s title wins over United, but held back his view on whether titles should be reassigned until the process is complete. Everton manager David Moyes questioned the contrast with punishments his club received in separate cases; Nottingham Forest manager Oliver Glasner also called for a timely final decision.

perspectives.body: Carrick’s account focuses on the personal cost of losing in the moment: he said a medal awarded years later could not restore the emotion of a title win. Moyes, meanwhile, raised the disparity between Everton’s past points deductions and the unresolved City case.

segments.title: The whistleblower remains protected
segments.body: Separately, Portugal has suspended the decision to remove Football Leaks founder Rui Pinto from witness protection. Pinto released documents that helped trigger the Premier League investigation into City. The Portuguese authorities will give him 10 days to assess a risk assessment that indicates a low threat to his safety; the decision to end his protection has not been settled.

content.headline: Northern Ireland’s World Cup hopes fade after 4-0 loss to Portugal
content.shortHeadline: Northern Ireland lose 4-0 to Portugal in play-off
content.standfirst: A first-leg defeat leaves Northern Ireland with a formidable task in Portugal on Tuesday. Manager Michael McArdle said overturning the four-goal deficit had gone from “improbable to impossible”.

sources.originalTitle: NI World Cup hopes gone from 'improbable to impossible'

segments.body: Northern Ireland lost 4-0 at home to Portugal in the first leg of their Women’s World Cup play-off semi-final. Telma Encarnacao scored a penalty, Jessica Silva and Rebecca Holloway’s own goal put Portugal 3-0 up by half-time, and Fatima Pinto added a fourth after Catarina Amado was sent off for Portugal. Northern Ireland’s Cora Chambers was also dismissed late on.

Manager Michael McArdle said the scoreline hurt and described the tie as having gone from “improbable to impossible”. He also said the match gave younger players valuable exposure. Northern Ireland travel to Portugal for Tuesday’s second leg and will be without Chambers, who was sent off in added time.

content.headline: Glasgow Warriors beat Connacht 36-19 to stay unbeaten in URC
content.shortHeadline: Glasgow beat Connacht 36-19 to maintain unbeaten start
content.standfirst: Glasgow scored five tries, including three from their driving maul, to earn a bonus-point win. Connacht rallied to within a score before Seb Stephen’s late try helped secure the result.

image.caption: Four of Glasgow’s five tries came from their rolling maul.

sources.originalTitle: Glasgow overpower Connacht to maintain unbeaten start

segments.body: Glasgow Warriors beat Connacht 36-19 at Scotstoun to maintain their unbeaten start to the United Rugby Championship season. Gregor Hiddleston scored twice, with Rory Darge, Josh McKay and Seb Stephen also crossing as Glasgow claimed a bonus point.

segments.title: Maul proves decisive
segments.body: Glasgow scored four of their five tries from rolling line-out mauls. Connacht’s Josh Ioane scored twice to cut the deficit to one score, but after substitute Josh Murphy was sin-binned for a high shot, Stephen finished another Glasgow maul to restore breathing room. Dan Lancaster added a late penalty.

content.headline: Maddinson’s 33-ball duck highlights Australia’s top-order struggles
content.shortHeadline: Maddinson makes 33-ball duck as Australia struggle
content.standfirst: Nic Maddinson’s return to Test cricket ended with a record-length duck for an Australian opener, as South Africa reduced Australia to 187-6 on day one in Durban. Matt Renshaw was unbeaten on 46.

image.caption: Nic Maddinson was recalled after a white-ball century for New South Wales.

sources.originalTitle: 33 balls, 0 runs - Maddinson's record amid Australia top-order struggles

segments.body: Nic Maddinson faced 33 balls without scoring before being bowled by Marco Jansen on his return to Test cricket against South Africa in Durban. It was the longest duck by an Australian Test opener and the third-longest by any Test opener. Australia ended day one at 187-6, with Matt Renshaw unbeaten on 46.

segments.title: Questions over selection and depth
segments.body: Maddinson returned to the side after treatment for testicular cancer, diagnosed in April 2025. His selection over 23-year-old Cooper Connolly had already prompted criticism from former Australia opener Matthew Hayden, who said selectors were “disrespecting first-class cricket”. The innings also intensified questions about Australia’s ageing batting line-up, although Renshaw’s late resistance offered some relief.

content.headline: Infantino appears set to run unopposed for another Fifa presidency
content.shortHeadline: Infantino may face no challenger in Fifa election
content.standfirst: With nominations due in November, senior figures believe Gianni Infantino may be unopposed in next year’s election. His critics have yet to settle on a challenger, while disputes over Fifa governance and a proposed commercial-rights plan continue.

image.caption: Gianni Infantino was first elected as Fifa president in 2016.

sources.originalTitle: Will anyone stop re-election of Infantino as Fifa president?

segments.body: Senior figures in world football believe Gianni Infantino may run unopposed for re-election as Fifa president, according to BBC Sport. The nomination deadline is 18 November, and the election is scheduled for 18 March in Rabat. Victor Montagliani, seen as a possible challenger, has said he intends to stand for re-election as Concacaf president instead.

segments.title: Opposition still unresolved
segments.body: The report describes a split between confederations over Infantino and his proposed Fifa Forward Enterprise plan to sell World Cup commercial rights to a private equity firm. Uefa had opposed the proposal and sought documents in US courts, but the report says it has not identified a candidate capable of uniting opposition. Any re-election remains a forecast, not a settled outcome.

content.headline: Jason Kelce swaps NFL for amateur rugby in London
content.shortHeadline: Jason Kelce turns out for London amateur rugby side
content.standfirst: The former Philadelphia Eagles centre joined Old Streetonians for a 30-minute match against Hackney RFC, surprising the amateur players. They said he adapted quickly to rugby’s physical demands and joined them for a post-match social.

image.caption: Jason Kelce and Beau Allen played for Old Streetonians against Hackney RFC.

sources.originalTitle: 'Ran through me' & 'good value in pub' - ex-NFL star Kelce tries rugby

segments.body: Former NFL centre Jason Kelce played for London amateur club Old Streetonians in a 30-minute friendly against Hackney RFC. Former Philadelphia Eagles team-mate Beau Allen joined him. Hackney players said Kelce initially had to adjust to rugby’s rules but quickly showed his strength and appetite for contact.

segments.title: A memorable post-match
segments.body: Kelce is in England to commentate on Philadelphia’s game against Jacksonville at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. Old Street chairman Will Gilgrass said Kelce and Allen stayed at a local pub after the match, chatting with players and taking part in the club’s initiation.

content.headline: The Avalanches turn jingles, old tech and memory into a new album and film
content.shortHeadline: The Avalanches make a wild album about memory
content.standfirst: On No Bad Memories, the sample collagists fold vintage jingles, technology sounds and an eclectic cast of collaborators into a restless new record. They also made a surreal short film with Haley Joel Osment.

image.caption: Robbie Chater of the Avalanches, who says the group’s music is built from the memories and humanity in sampled sounds.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Spend time going down rabbit holes’: how the Avalanches created their wildest album yet

segments.body: The Avalanches’ new album, No Bad Memories, turns the sounds of old technology, advertising and children’s TV into a bright, fast-moving collage. The Australian duo say they wanted a joyous record, but its central idea is unsettling: how jingles and electronic sounds can shape and distort what we remember.

segments.title: A record that keeps skipping ahead
segments.body: The album moves between collaborators including John Glacier, Khadija Al Hanafi, Panda Bear and Haruomi Hosono. Chater and Di Blasi also made a 35-minute film, with Haley Joel Osment as an archivist whose own memories become entangled with the material he collects. The band say that clearing samples has become increasingly difficult and costly, even as they return to digging for more.

content.headline: As punk turns 50, musicians around the world explain what it means to them
content.shortHeadline: Punk at 50: musicians on the freedom to question everything
content.standfirst: From a Ukrainian medic-turned-musician to punk scenes in Morocco, South Africa, India and China, artists describe how the genre gives them a language for anger, community and resistance.

image.caption: Musicians from Beton, Twenty One Children, Taqbir and Depustūtes, among the artists reflecting on punk’s reach.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It gave me a superpower – question everything’: ​as punk turns 50, bands from China to Greenland explain how it fires up their lives

segments.body: Punk’s reach is not limited to the places where it first took hold. Musicians from Ukraine, Morocco, South Africa, India, Latvia, China and Greenland describe finding their own versions of the music—and using it to challenge authority, prejudice and the pressure to fit in.

segments.title: A scene built on local ties
segments.body: For Beton’s Andriy Zholob, guitars offered relief during frontline medical service, and his band recorded a Clash cover to raise money for Ukrainian resistance. In Soweto, Twenty One Children’s Abdula Skink connects punk to skating, community work and a DIY skate park. Other musicians describe the risks of performing anonymously or speaking openly about politics.

content.headline: Liz Harris finds a restorative kind of togetherness with Helen
content.shortHeadline: Liz Harris on Helen, collaboration and music-industry scams
content.standfirst: The Grouper musician discusses the contrast between her solitary work and the brighter, collaborative sound of Helen, as well as the royalty fraud that followed a song’s unexpected viral success.

image.caption: Liz Harris, whose work as Grouper is largely solitary and whose band Helen brings a more collaborative side into view.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s rational to fear the music industry’: Grouper’s Liz Harris on virality, streaming scammers and her ‘restorative’ dream-pop trio

segments.body: Liz Harris is used to making music alone as Grouper. In Helen, her dream-pop trio with Jed Bindeman and Scott Simmons, the collaboration brings a different kind of energy. Harris says rehearsing and playing with friends helped lift her spirits while she was dealing with medical difficulties; their second album, Linda’s Head, makes that shared presence audible.

segments.title: When a song goes viral
segments.body: A TikTok revival of Grouper’s 2008 song Poison Tree brought new listeners, but Harris says someone else had fraudulently registered and uploaded it, collecting royalties before she and her label manager were able to shut down the scam and recover what she was owed. She remains wary of streaming platforms’ ability to police impersonation and infringing tracks.

content.headline: Soft Cell’s final album became a farewell to Dave Ball
content.shortHeadline: Marc Almond on Soft Cell’s final album and Dave Ball
content.standfirst: Soft Cell had finished Danceteria when keyboardist Dave Ball died two days later. Marc Almond reflects on a last record shaped by their time in New York and a partnership that lasted nearly five decades.

image.caption: Marc Almond and Dave Ball of Soft Cell, whose album Danceteria became their final record together.

sources.originalTitle: Soft Cell’s Marc Almond: ‘We finished the album – two days later Dave passed away’

segments.body: Soft Cell agreed that their new album was finished in October 2025. Two days later, Marc Almond was told that Dave Ball had died. Danceteria is the duo’s sixth and final album: Almond says he would not make another Soft Cell record without his longtime bandmate.

segments.title: New York, then and now
segments.body: The record looks back to the pair’s early-1980s New York life, with its clubs, experimentation and excess, while also making room for loneliness and the impact of the AIDS crisis. Almond describes the album as a fitting full circle: the two had become closer during its making, and Ball was happy with the finished record.

content.headline: Tom Morello’s first solo rock album turns family history into protest
content.shortHeadline: Tom Morello on protest, family and his first solo rock album
content.standfirst: On Everyone Gets What They Want, the Rage Against the Machine guitarist brings his long-running activism to a first full-length solo rock record. He also reflects on how his mother shaped his politics.

image.caption: Tom Morello, whose new solo album continues his use of music as political activism.

sources.originalTitle: Tom Morello on Rage Against the Machine fans turning against him

segments.body: Tom Morello describes Everyone Gets What They Want as an anti-racist, anti-fascist record for people who have had enough. His first full-length solo rock album puts him at the microphone with the heavy guitar sound associated with Rage Against the Machine, alongside guests including Serj Tankian, Kneecap and his son Roman.

segments.title: A lesson carried forward
segments.body: Morello traces his political outlook to his mother, Mary, who stood up against racism and supported causes from anti-colonial movements to workers’ rights. He recalls her explaining, during a grape boycott when he was six, why their family would go without grapes to support farm workers. He says that belief in ordinary people’s ability to act runs through his songs.

content.headline: Dawn Richard brings New Orleans’ musical blend home on creole culture
content.shortHeadline: Dawn Richard’s New Orleans celebration on creole culture
content.standfirst: The final instalment of Richard’s hometown trilogy trades some of her past experimental edge for a communal, genre-crossing sound. The review finds its warmth compelling, even when the songwriting feels less adventurous.

sources.originalTitle: creole culture

segments.body: On creole culture, Dawn Richard draws on New Orleans through live instrumentation, programmed beats and shifting styles. The album completes a trilogy that began with new breed and continued with Second Line: An Electro Revival, but the review hears a more understated approach to the city’s musical and cultural mix.

segments.title: A lively procession, with limits
segments.body: Songs move between jazz, bounce, reggae, amapiano, gospel and electronic production, often flowing into one another like a DJ set. The review praises the record’s communal pulse and Richard’s versatility, while arguing that a more grounded, less provocative mode leaves some of her eccentric imagination untapped.

content.headline: Cameron Winter’s Carnegie Hall concert becomes a solo live triumph
content.shortHeadline: Cameron Winter turns a Carnegie Hall night into a live album
content.standfirst: The Geese frontman’s solo set reworks songs from Heavy Metal alongside new material, revealing a more open, piano-led performer. The review weighs the music’s intimacy against the mythmaking around the concert.

sources.originalTitle: Live at Carnegie Hall

segments.body: Live at Carnegie Hall captures Cameron Winter’s December 2025 solo performance, including three unreleased songs and material from Heavy Metal. The review hears the songs loosen and breathe in this piano-led setting, with Winter’s shifting pace and touch bringing a new sense of control to music that was more fraught on his studio debut.

segments.title: A concert and its legend
segments.body: The album accompanies a concert film by Paul Thomas Anderson, and the review notes how both preserve the performance while adding to its mythology. It singles out “If You Turn Back Now” and the new songs as highlights, while suggesting Winter’s evasiveness may be a way of protecting himself from the pressure of rising fame.

content.headline: The Beatles’ Rubber Soul reissue brings the album’s contradictions into focus
content.shortHeadline: Rubber Soul, heard again in an expansive new reissue
content.standfirst: A new deluxe edition gathers alternate mixes, outtakes and studio detail around the Beatles’ pivotal 1965 album. The review argues that its changing versions reveal a work shaped by both artistic ambition and commercial circumstance.

sources.originalTitle: Rubber Soul (Super Deluxe)

segments.body: Rubber Soul arrived at a turning point for the Beatles and for pop, with its songs reaching beyond the group’s earlier approach. This expanded edition brings together UK and US versions, mono and stereo mixes, outtakes and a new remix, giving listeners several ways to hear the record’s development.

segments.title: No single definitive version
segments.body: The review finds the box set most persuasive when it exposes what changed between takes and releases, from the album’s track lists to its mixes. Rather than treating Rubber Soul as a fixed monument, it presents a work made under deadline and industry pressure by musicians still experimenting—and suggests listeners’ preferred version may depend on how they first heard it.

content.headline: Peter Greenaway’s unfinished film is caught in a dispute over its final cut
content.shortHeadline: Peter Greenaway’s film is stuck in a post-production dispute
content.standfirst: Three years after filming began in Tuscany, Greenaway’s assisted-dying drama remains unfinished amid a dispute with producers over the cut and the film’s rights. The city of Lucca says it has not received answers about the project’s delay.

image.caption: Peter Greenaway, whose film Tower Stories remains caught in a dispute over its completion and release.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Is death necessary?’: why Peter Greenaway’s assisted dying drama is stuck in post-production hell

segments.body: Peter Greenaway’s film, now called Tower Stories, was conceived as a drama about mortality, featuring Dustin Hoffman as a New York writer returning to his roots in Lucca, Italy. Production was delayed and ran over budget; after an initial assembly was delivered, the director and producers reportedly diverged over which version should be completed and released.

segments.title: A project in limbo
segments.body: The Guardian reports that two unfinished cuts are in circulation and that a dispute over rights remains unresolved. Facing East, the production company, did not respond to requests for comment. Lucca councillor Remo Santini says the city supported the shoot and had seen a preview, but has had no subsequent explanation from the production or director.

content.headline: The Social Reckoning puts Facebook under scrutiny, but critics differ on its aim
content.shortHeadline: The Social Reckoning: a chilling story, or a drama without bite?
content.standfirst: Aaron Sorkin’s sequel draws on reporting about Facebook’s internal practices and whistleblower Frances Haugen. One review finds a frightening portrait of social media’s reach; another argues the film lacks the tension to change anyone’s mind.

image.caption: Jeremy Strong plays Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.

sources.originalTitle: I was terrified watching The Social Reckoning – then went back to scrolling
The new Darth Vader: how tech execs became the film villains of our age
The Social Reckoning review: Aaron Sorkin's drama puts Facebook on trial, but it won't change anyone's minds ★★☆☆☆

segments.body: The Social Reckoning follows Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz and former Facebook employee Frances Haugen as they investigate the company’s internal research and the effects of its platform. Jeremy Strong plays Mark Zuckerberg, while the film’s account of the Facebook Files turns the focus from the company’s origins to its influence and accountability.

segments.title: Two readings of the film
segments.body: The i’s review calls the film a chilling exploration of how social media has reshaped society, while also reflecting on how difficult it can be to stop using Meta’s products. The Guardian’s piece focuses on the change in public perception of Zuckerberg and notes that former employees found parts of Strong’s portrayal recognisable. The BBC’s review, by contrast, judges the drama repetitive and too undramatic to shift viewers’ views.

perspectives.body: The BBC review argues that the film’s lack of danger and dramatic conflict undermines its investigative premise, and that the company’s continued power makes a decisive reckoning feel out of reach.

content.headline: Artificial turns the story of OpenAI into a warning about control and risk
content.shortHeadline: Artificial asks who gets to control AI’s future
content.standfirst: Luca Guadagnino’s drama follows OpenAI’s formation and the conflict between Sam Altman and Ilya Sutskever. Its account of safety, ambition and commercial pressure has gained fresh resonance, though the film’s treatment of Altman is criticised as thin.

sources.originalTitle: AI fears are growing – and unsettling new film Artificial puts them, and the future of humanity, centre stage

segments.body: Artificial traces the formation of OpenAI as a non-profit and its transformation into the company behind ChatGPT. Andrew Garfield plays Altman and Yura Borisov plays Sutskever, whose split over the company’s direction becomes a story about idealism, commercial priorities and who should control powerful AI systems.

segments.title: Off-screen questions
segments.body: The film’s release was complicated when Amazon MGM Studios, which financed it, said it would not distribute the picture; Neon later acquired it. The gathered account notes that Amazon had invested in a partnership with OpenAI, while Altman said he had not spoken with Amazon about the decision. The film’s critique of the industry arrives without any practical, industry-wide safety resolution in sight.

content.headline: Martin McDonagh and his stars discuss guilt, history and Wild Horse Nine
content.shortHeadline: Wild Horse Nine: McDonagh, Malkovich and Rockwell on the film
content.standfirst: John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell play CIA agents stationed on Easter Island in 1973 in Martin McDonagh’s new film. Their conversation ranges from the story’s atmosphere of regret to the actors’ working relationship and McDonagh’s take on political secrecy.

image.caption: Martin McDonagh with actors Sam Rockwell and John Malkovich, who star in Wild Horse Nine.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Old-timey fascism was kept secret. Now you don’t have to hide it’: Martin McDonagh, John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell on Wild Horse Nine

segments.body: Wild Horse Nine follows two CIA agents played by John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell, sent to Rapa Nui after plotting the 1973 coup in Chile. McDonagh says he began writing with “GUILT and REGRET” in mind; the film mixes the director’s familiar odd-couple humour with a more mournful focus on age, death and the past.

segments.title: Two actors, two approaches
segments.body: Rockwell is openly admiring of Malkovich, while Malkovich describes the intensive rehearsals they shared. Their conversation also turns to the film’s treatment of political power and secrecy. McDonagh says covert interventions have become more brazen, but cautions against treating one president as uniquely responsible for the history of US actions abroad.

content.headline: The Lost Children of Tuam recounts a tragedy without easy closure
content.shortHeadline: The Lost Children of Tuam tells a painful story with restraint
content.standfirst: Monica Dolan plays historian Catherine Corless in a drama about the children who died at St Mary’s mother and baby home. The review praises its serious, unsentimental approach to the discoveries and the survivors’ testimony.

image.caption: Monica Dolan as Catherine Corless in The Lost Children of Tuam.

sources.originalTitle: The Lost Children of Tuam review – deeply serious retelling of Ireland’s devastating tragedy

segments.body: The Lost Children of Tuam follows Catherine Corless as she investigates deaths at St Mary’s mother and baby home in County Galway. Her research uncovered death certificates for nearly 800 children but no burial records. The film presents the scale of the tragedy without adding a consoling resolution.

The review praises Monica Dolan’s portrayal of Corless and notes the force of brief appearances by survivors, now middle-aged, who describe lives marked by neglect and abuse. Its account is deliberately restrained, resisting the urge to make a devastating history feel like a neatly resolved drama.

content.headline: Ali G returns with a question about the future of character comedy
content.shortHeadline: Can Ali G revive character comedy for the big screen?
content.standfirst: Sacha Baron Cohen’s return to Ali G raises questions about whether the character’s satire still works in a more polarised Britain. The argument reaches beyond one film to a genre that has struggled to find a place in cinemas.

image.caption: Sacha Baron Cohen as Ali G in Ali G: Who Iz I?

sources.originalTitle: Can Ali G: Who Iz I? save character comedy cinema?

segments.body: Ali G: Who Iz I? brings Sacha Baron Cohen’s character back to the screen, but the film’s relevance is not yet clear. Ali G’s comedy once drew on assumptions about race and popular culture; the piece asks whether those targets still land, or risk reinforcing the caricatures the character was meant to expose.

segments.title: A form in search of an audience
segments.body: The argument places Ali G in a tradition of persona-driven comedy, from Peter Sellers to Austin Powers and Borat. Its future may depend on whether a comic character can still speak to shared social references in a fractured culture. The film’s trailer offers little evidence yet of how Baron Cohen has updated the character’s approach.

content.headline: Animals gives Ben Affleck’s kidnapping thriller little room to breathe
content.shortHeadline: Animals: Ben Affleck’s thriller is short on tension
content.standfirst: A strong cast and a high-stakes kidnapping plot promise a propulsive political thriller, but the review finds Affleck’s new film listless and visually anonymous, with too little to say about Los Angeles.

image.caption: Kerry Washington and Ben Affleck in Animals.

sources.originalTitle: Animals review – Ben Affleck’s dull Netflix thriller is lacking in bark and bite

segments.body: Ben Affleck plays a Los Angeles mayoral candidate whose son is kidnapped on election night. The ransom, a divided family and an enigmatic fixer create the makings of a tense thriller, but the review says much of the action stays inside the family’s wealthy home and circles through arguments without building momentum.

The review also compares the film’s kidnapping plot with Spike Lee’s Highest 2 Lowest, arguing that Animals offers little sense of how its setting changes the material. Gillian Anderson is singled out for committing to a pulpy tone, but the film’s final set-piece and slick visual style leave the critic unconvinced.

content.headline: Sofia Coppola reflects on Lost in Translation and Marie Antoinette
content.shortHeadline: Sofia Coppola on her films, family and the details she notices
content.standfirst: In a conversation with a young aspiring filmmaker, Coppola recalls filming in Tokyo, the teenage perspective behind Marie Antoinette’s soundtrack and the women in her family who shaped how she sees the world.

image.caption: Sofia Coppola at the Venice film festival in 2025.

sources.originalTitle: Sofia Coppola: ‘I’m glad we weren’t kicked out of Tokyo making Lost in Translation’

segments.body: Sofia Coppola says her mother taught her to follow her interests and notice the beauty in ordinary surroundings—an influence she sees in the details of her films. Looking back on Lost in Translation, she recalls filming a few scenes in Tokyo without permission, including moments on a subway and at Shibuya Crossing.

Coppola says she chose contemporary post-punk and new romantic music for Marie Antoinette because the young queen’s age reminded her of her own teenage listening. She also discusses her mother’s behind-the-scenes footage of the film and her continuing pleasure in visiting film sets, where she says she is still impressed by movie-making.

content.headline: Doctor Who faces an uncertain future after its Disney+ partnership ends
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who’s future is uncertain after the Disney+ deal ends
content.standfirst: The BBC has cancelled a planned Christmas special and is seeking a new funding partner, leaving the long-running series without a confirmed next Doctor. Fans and contributors disagree about what went wrong, but want the show back on screen.

image.caption: An illustration showing several of Doctor Who’s incarnations, including Jodie Whittaker and Ncuti Gatwa.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: Doctor Who has been off air since its most recent series ended in 2025. The BBC has ended its partnership with Disney+, cancelled a planned Christmas special and put future production out to competitive tender. No replacement Doctor or new partner has been announced, leaving the show’s next steps unclear.

segments.title: A changing institution
segments.body: The feature traces the show’s history of reinvention, from its 2005 revival through successive Doctors and showrunners. Contributors point to uneven scripts and declining viewing figures, while also noting the abuse faced by Jodie Whittaker and Ncuti Gatwa. Lifelong fan Frank Skinner says the series needs to return without losing its core values of kindness and curiosity.

content.headline: The Split Up brings a new British Asian family into the divorce drama
content.shortHeadline: The Split Up moves the family-law drama to Manchester
content.standfirst: The spin-off moves the glossy legal series from London to Manchester, with Ritu Arya leading a British Asian cast. Its writers and producers explain how the show aims to keep the original’s family melodrama while making the new family its own.

image.caption: Ritu Arya leads the cast of The Split Up, the Manchester-set spin-off of The Split.

sources.originalTitle: The Split is back – with a twist

segments.body: The Split Up follows Aria Kishan, played by Ritu Arya, as she prepares to take over her family’s Manchester law firm. Her plans are unsettled by her father’s change of direction, a former partner joining the firm and the death of her mother. Like The Split, the series mixes divorce cases with turmoil at home.

segments.title: A new family, a familiar format
segments.body: Writer Ursula Rani Sarma says she wanted British Asian characters living ordinary, recognisable lives rather than being defined by exceptional circumstances. The series has a predominantly British Asian cast and creative team. Original creator Abi Morgan says its family-centred melodrama remains, while the new writers shape a distinct setting and tone.

content.headline: Romola Garai on Adultery, marital disappointment and filming intimacy
content.shortHeadline: Romola Garai on the questions behind ITV drama Adultery
content.standfirst: Garai plays a married personal trainer drawn into an affair in Danny Brocklehurst’s new drama. She discusses the story’s portrayal of women, intimacy coordination and the family pressures that shape her character.

image.caption: Romola Garai in ITV drama Adultery.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I’ve hit my midlife sexpot era!’ Romola Garai on marital misery, cheating … and sex scenes in cars

segments.body: Adultery centres on Beth, played by Romola Garai, and GP Tom, played by Dominic Cooper, who begin an affair after their teenage children start dating. Garai says the script’s attention to marital disappointment and a woman who has suppressed parts of herself persuaded her to take on a story about infidelity.

segments.title: Making intimate scenes
segments.body: Garai describes how intimacy coordinators now help actors plan sex scenes with clear, technical conversations and a designated person responsible for performers’ comfort. She also hopes the drama shows the consequences of the affair for spouses and children, rather than treating it as consequence-free scandal.

content.headline: Carrie’s new TV adaptation divides critics over what to change
content.shortHeadline: Carrie: two critics disagree over the new adaptation
content.standfirst: The Prime Video series has prompted debate about how it changes Stephen King’s angry, bullied teenager. One account sees an inventive update; another argues it strips away Carrie’s agency and the force of her revenge.

image.caption: Summer H Howell as Carrie in the new Prime Video adaptation.

sources.originalTitle: The Carrie remake made me furious
Why a new TV version of horror classic Carrie is already annoying people

segments.body: Mike Flanagan’s eight-part Carrie moves the story into the present day and makes significant changes to its characters and backstory. In a strongly critical review, The i argues that the new version turns Carrie into a frightened figure with little control, and softens both her mother and the people who torment her.

segments.title: The adaptation debate
segments.body: The BBC’s account also reports fans’ objections to Carrie’s casting and to screen versions that soften the character. It presents a counterpoint from horror scholar Sorcha Ní Fhlainn, who says the new series codes Carrie’s otherness through her home-schooling and clothes, and sees the adaptation as a modern story about bullying and social media. The BBC ultimately praises the series; The i rejects its reinvention.

perspectives.body: The BBC’s account argues that the series works on its own terms as a layered contemporary horror and coming-of-age story, despite changes that have frustrated some book fans.

content.headline: Frasier’s Jane Leeves and David Hyde Pierce revisit Daphne and Niles
content.shortHeadline: Frasier’s Jane Leeves and David Hyde Pierce on Daphne and Niles
content.standfirst: The actors look back on the sitcom’s seven-season slow-burn romance, from a much-loved tango to the audience’s reaction when the pair finally kissed. Their friendship off-screen also endured after the series ended.

image.caption: Daphne and Niles, played by Jane Leeves and David Hyde Pierce in Frasier.

sources.originalTitle: ‘He was devastatingly sexy’: Frasier’s Jane Leeves and David Hyde Pierce on the love between Daphne and Niles

segments.body: Jane Leeves and David Hyde Pierce recall how Daphne and Niles’ relationship developed from a one-sided crush into a long-running will-they-won’t-they story. They discuss the humour and patience in the writing, including the candlelit tango in “Moon Dance” and the moment the characters finally kissed.

segments.title: A partnership beyond the show
segments.body: The actors say the cast became close, and they have remained friends since Frasier ended. Leeves and Hyde Pierce also reflect on how the writers ended the romantic suspense before it wore thin, while Leeves wishes the show had handled her pregnancy differently instead of concealing it with a weight-gain storyline.

content.headline: Bake Off’s audience-choice week gives the tent a welcome shake-up
content.shortHeadline: Bake Off lets viewers set the challenges—and loosens its rules
content.standfirst: The series gave viewers control of the baking tasks for the first time, producing unusual challenges and a sharper tone. The review argues that a little more unpredictability could help refresh the familiar format.

image.caption: Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood judge a week of Bake Off challenges chosen by viewers.

sources.originalTitle: Bake Off is toughening up. Good

segments.body: In Bake Off’s first audience-choice week, viewers set the challenges instead of judges Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood. Bakers made cheesecake with family members, different technical bakes from the same basic cupboard and a wearable showstopper—an experiment that brought more uncertainty into the tent.

The episode was not especially chaotic, but the review welcomes the change and a more openly combative dynamic between Lawson and Hollywood. It also notes a harder edge in the judging, arguing that the programme can keep its warmth while moving beyond the cosy formula that has come to feel dated.

content.headline: Gromit will speak for the first time, in Martin Freeman’s audiobook reading
content.shortHeadline: Martin Freeman gives Gromit an audiobook voice
content.standfirst: The famously silent Wallace & Gromit dog will be heard for the first time in an audiobook of his autobiography. Creator Nick Park says Martin Freeman will read Gromit’s thoughts rather than invent a new speaking voice for him.

image.caption: Gromit, the famously silent dog whose autobiography will be read by Martin Freeman.

sources.originalTitle: Gromit finally gets a voice … and it’s Martin Freeman

segments.body: After 37 years on screen without a spoken word, Gromit will have an audiobook voice: Martin Freeman will read Grand: The Autobiography of Gromit. Animator Nick Park says Freeman will not create a conventional Gromit voice, but will deliver the character’s inner thoughts and wry observations.
The book is due on 22 October. A separate behind-the-scenes experience, Larger Than Life, is also planned for London’s Lightroom, opening on 14 October.

content.headline: Jerry Hall’s unpredictable Traitors game makes her an agent of chaos
content.shortHeadline: Jerry Hall is The Celebrity Traitors’ wild card
content.standfirst: Hall’s impulsive choices and baffling comments have made her an unlikely standout on The Celebrity Traitors. The review argues that her apparent disregard for the game is precisely what makes her compelling.

image.caption: Jerry Hall with fellow contestants on The Celebrity Traitors.

sources.originalTitle: Jerry Hall deserves murder on Celebrity Traitors – but legends live beyond logic

segments.body: Jerry Hall has repeatedly acted against the logic of The Celebrity Traitors, including shouting “haggis” almost immediately during a mission where players could choose to be released at the risk of being murdered. Rather than making her an easy target, the review says her unpredictability has become the show’s source of chaos.

Hall’s unexplained outbursts leave fellow contestants and viewers guessing whether she has a strategy at all. The review suggests that her confidence and extraordinary life have insulated her from the usual pressures of the game—and make it impossible to predict what she will do next.

content.headline: A £350 GTA collector’s box highlights gaming’s growing price barrier
content.shortHeadline: The £350 GTA box points to gaming’s luxury-price problem
content.standfirst: Rockstar’s Grand Theft Auto VI collector’s box does not include the game, which brings the combined cost to £420. The argument is not that merchandise should not exist, but that console gaming increasingly caters to people able to pay more.

image.caption: Grand Theft Auto VI’s Vice City collector’s box, sold separately from the game.

sources.originalTitle: What the £350 Grand Theft Auto ‘collector’s box’ says about the escalating cost of gaming

segments.body: Rockstar’s £350 Grand Theft Auto VI: The Goodtime State – Vice City Collection includes merchandise, but no game or download code. Add the £70 game and the total reaches £420. The writer, a collector who enjoys special editions, argues that the price is striking even by the standards of gaming merchandise.

segments.title: A widening divide
segments.body: The piece connects expensive merchandise to rising console and game costs, suggesting that high-end gaming is increasingly aimed at a smaller group of players with more money to spend. It contrasts that market with the much larger number of people who play free or low-cost games on mobile, and worries that the kinds of games built as expansive worlds are becoming less accessible.

content.headline: Ace Combat 8 delivers thrilling dogfights and a surprisingly moving story
content.shortHeadline: Ace Combat 8 makes arcade flying exhilarating
content.standfirst: The latest entry builds on the series’ accessible, high-speed combat with a more cinematic story and spectacular skies. The review finds its missions thrilling, even if the battle can become confusing and the innovations are incremental.

image.caption: A fighter jet cuts through the skies in Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve.

sources.originalTitle: Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve review – brilliant aerial combat game fulfils the Top Gun fantasy

segments.body: Ace Combat 8 puts players in the role of a pilot whose reputation began as propaganda, then becomes real as the conflict escalates. Its accessible controls, varied missions and beautifully rendered skies make dogfighting feel immediate, with the game leaning into the cinematic rush that has long been part of the series.

segments.title: Combat takes centre stage
segments.body: The review praises the weight of the weapons, the destructible environments and the frantic missions, but says visual clutter can make objectives hard to track. The story also borrows from Top Gun: Maverick, yet its presentation and character work make the reviewer unexpectedly invested. Online multiplayer could not be tested during the review period.

content.headline: Silver Pines turns familiar noir and horror influences into a vivid game world
